qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

The Commission is proposing the gradual inclusion of municipal waste incineration plants in the EU ETS from 2031. Local authorities and industry organisations in Poland are warning of increases in waste collection charges and heating bills. They point out that these increases could reach over 50 %. For years, local authorities in Poland have invested in modern incinerators equipped with advanced flue gas treatment systems. These facilities process waste that cannot be recycled, reduce the need for landfill and generate heat and electricity. Now the Commission wants to impose additional costs on them. Residents are therefore set to pay more for using solutions designed to protect the environment. EU policy forcing the introduction of a deposit-refund scheme has led to rising waste collection charges in Poland. The inclusion of incineration plants in the ETS poses the threat of further price rises. 1.
By how much, according to the Commission’s calculations, will the inclusion of incineration plants in the ETS increase waste collection charges and heating bills in Poland?
What specific environmental benefits does the Commission expect from including incineration plants in the ETS, given that the purchase of allowances will not make nonrecyclable waste disappear?

Has the Commission assessed how many residents will be unable to afford to heat their houses and flats as a result of these price rises, and what impact could the increase in energy poverty have on their health and the number of premature deaths?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.11.2026) Municipal waste incineration represents a significant and growing source of fossil CO₂. Gradually bringing this sector into the Emissions Trading System (ETS)1 aims to reduce these emissions while supporting the transition towards a more circular economy, complementing waste policies and supporting the Clean Industrial Deal2 objectives to accelerate circularity and decarbonisation. Only around 20% of plastic waste is being recycled, separate collection of recyclables remains overall low, and up to 70% of residual waste consists of recyclables3. A harmonised price signal supports Member States’ binding recycling targets by improving the business case for waste prevention, separate collection, sorting and recycling. It also supports the carbon capture roll-out through the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank. This can substantially reduce incineration emissions by up to 53 million tonnes CO2 over the next decade and generate recycled materials displacing more carbon-intensive virgin materials4. The Commission is strongly committed to ensuring a smooth transition, balancing the economic and environmental benefits of circularity, such as reduced dependence on imported primary materials and lower production costs, with the costs of waste management. While projected costs are assessed to range between EUR 1-2,5 per household per month for unsorted residual waste5 on average, the proposal mitigates immediate costs through a gradual introduction of obligations, free allocation for waste-to-energy district heating and priority national ETS revenue use to improve waste prevention, collection and recycling in line with the waste hierarchy.

1 COM/2026/616 final. 2 COM/2025/85 final. 3 SWD(2026) 616 final, part 4/5, Annex 13, p. 83 and 95. 4 SWD(2026) 616 final, part 1/5, Section 6.1.1.8., and part 4/5, Annex 13, Section 1.3. 5 SWD(2026) 616 final, part 4/5, Annex 13, Sections 1.3. and 1.7.3.4.
